questions.q: What does `torch.autocast` do during the forward pass?
options: It converts the entire model to float16 with no exceptions
It automatically runs numerically safe ops like matrix multiplies in reduced precision while keeping sensitive ops in float32
It disables GPU execution and runs on CPU instead
It permanently changes the model's saved weights to float16
questions.explain: Autocast selects precision per operation — reduced precision for numerically safe, compute-heavy ops, and float32 for operations sensitive to precision loss.

questions.q: Why does float16 training typically require `GradScaler`?
options: GradScaler speeds up the forward pass
Float16's small exponent range means small gradients can underflow to exactly zero during backpropagation; scaling the loss up beforehand keeps them representable
GradScaler converts float16 to float32 automatically with no other purpose
Without it, PyTorch cannot allocate GPU memory
questions.explain: Loss scaling pushes small gradient values away from float16's underflow range during backward, and GradScaler automates scaling up before backward and unscaling before the optimizer step.

questions.q: Why doesn't bfloat16 generally need a GradScaler?
options: Bfloat16 cannot be used for training at all
Bfloat16 has the same exponent range as float32, avoiding the gradient underflow problem that float16 has, at the cost of reduced mantissa precision
Bfloat16 automatically runs on Tensor Cores only
GradScaler is only compatible with CPUs
questions.explain: Bfloat16 shares float32's wide exponent range, so small gradients don't underflow to zero the way they can in float16, removing the need for loss scaling.

questions.q: What does `scaler.step(optimizer)` do if it detects an overflow (inf/NaN) in the gradients?
options: It crashes the training run immediately
It skips that optimizer step entirely, avoiding corrupting the model weights, rather than applying the bad gradients
It automatically switches the model to float64
It silently applies the overflowed gradients anyway
questions.explain: `scaler.step()` checks for overflow caused by scaling and skips the optimizer update for that iteration if detected, protecting the weights from corruption.

questions.q: Why is mixed precision primarily a speedup for compute-bound operations rather than memory-bound ones?
options: Mixed precision only works on CPU-bound code
The largest gains come from GEMM-heavy, compute-bound layers that run on Tensor Cores in reduced precision; memory-bound elementwise ops see a smaller relative benefit
Memory-bound operations cannot be represented in float16
Compute-bound operations are unaffected by precision changes
questions.explain: Tensor Cores accelerate the compute-heavy matrix multiply pattern specifically, so compute-bound, GEMM-heavy ops see the largest speedup from mixed precision.
